title: Hasan al-Basri to the caliph
hookLine: a preacher writes to the caliph: the just ruler is like a shepherd
tomorrow: what makes someone leave home alone, not knowing when he'll return?

cards: The new caliph has a request, and he sends it to Basra, to a preacher known for not flattering anyone. Describe the just ruler for me, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz writes. A ruler asking that could be fishing for praise.
The preacher, Hasan al-Basri, picks up his pen, and the picture he sends back isn't a palace or a throne. It's a man out in the open with his animals, watching the weather.

teach.h: A SUPPORT FOR EVERYONE WHO LEANS.
teach.b: Know, Commander of the Faithful, Hasan writes, in the letter as Ibn Abd Rabbih keeps it: God made the just ruler a support for everyone who leans and a straightening for everyone who strays.

The just ruler is like a shepherd, tender to his camels, who looks for the best pasture for them, keeps them from places where they'd perish, guards them from wild animals and shields them from heat and cold.

He's like a father, tender to his children. He's like a mother, gentle and caring, who carried the child and nursed it, who wakes when it wakes. And he's the heart among the limbs: when it's sound, they're sound.
Notice who the subject is. Not the shepherd's glory. The pasture, the cold, the danger.
He's measured by what happens to the flock.

teach.h: EACH OF YOU IS A SHEPHERD.
teach.b: Behind the picture is a hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim: each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock.
The ruler, the man of a household, the woman in her home, even a servant with his master's wealth. So the picture isn't only for caliphs.
Everybody is watching over somebody: a little brother, a team, a parent getting older.

how: Hasan al-Basri's letter is retold in Muslim writing on just rule, and the hadith 'each of you is a shepherd' is taught to children and adults as a duty of care in every home.

games.q: what does “hasan al-basri to the caliph” mean?
o: a preacher's letter picturing the just ruler as a shepherd
a caliph's letter dismissing a preacher for his sermons
a sermon warning the caliph about losing a war

games.q: Hasan's pictures of the just ruler — tap the pairs.
p: when sound, the limbs are sound

s: Hasan's letter flatters the caliph with a portrait of his greatness
it measures the ruler by the flock: pasture, danger, heat and cold.
in the hadith, only rulers are called shepherds
each of you is a shepherd: ruler, household, even a servant with his master's wealth.
Hasan also compares the just ruler to a mother
who carried the child, nursed it and wakes when it wakes.

games.q: your older brother leaves for college, and suddenly you're the oldest at home. what fits the shepherd's care?
o: notice what the younger ones need, and quietly cover it.
announce you're in charge now, so they'll listen.
nothing changes; looking after others is a parent's job.
games.why: the hadith makes everyone a shepherd of someone, and Hasan's shepherd is measured by the flock's needs, not by his own title.

practice: Look at a photo of the people you look after, or just their names in your phone: a sibling, a friend, a team, a parent getting older. Rest your eyes on one face for the whole sit.
If you pray, you can keep them in mind before God; if not, notice one need of theirs you hadn't seen.

wordCard.voice: Hasan al-Basri to the caliph: the preacher's letter picturing the just ruler as a shepherd, a father, a mother and a heart.

orig.note: Arabic: ra'i, shepherd, the word in the hadith 'each of you is a shepherd'.

carryVoice: For the road: the shepherd's care, measured by how the flock is doing. Day 1646, tended.

sources.ref: Hasan al-Basri's letter to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz on the just imam, in Ibn Abd Rabbih, al-'Iqd al-Farid
Sahih al-Bukhari 893; Sahih Muslim 1829 (each of you is a shepherd and each is responsible for his flock)
